newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland's rulers on tightrope over flood relief.
newsitem.headline: Poland's rulers on tightrope over flood relief.

text.p: As receding floods in south Poland revealed shattered towns and villages, the government on Tuesday faced tough choices over how to rebuild without further battering the economy or its own political prospects.
In hardest-hit parts of the south water drained away but many centres including much of the major cities of Wroclaw and Opole were still inundated.
Other communities along the raging Odra were still bracing to face the devastation wrought by a huge surge of high water relentlessly rolling north to the German border and the sea.
In the fine riverside town of Glogow residents, warned by terrifying images on television of the catastrophe in the south, were taking no chances as water seeped in through dykes.
"People are evacuating themselves. After the experience of people in the south, they are taking their things and going," said central crisis committee spokesman Krzysztof Pomes.

The floods caused by days of downpours early last week have struck dozens of towns and hundreds of villages, killing 36 people. The region's worst natural disaster in centuries also wrought suffering and death in the neighbouring Czech Republic.
Poland's coalition cabinet was meeting to decide proposals for changes to the 1997 budget and other laws that will be put to an emergency sitting of parliament on Wednesday.
It has already raised hundreds of millions of dollars by yanking current budget funds from other purposes and freezing all state capital construction projects.

Now it wants to increase the amount the law allows it to borrow at home and abroad, so it can get a $300 million soft loan from the World Bank and borrow up to one billion zlotys ($300 million) from Poland's central bank.
Foreign currency markets were jittery over any possible impact on Poland's swollen budget deficit and the zloty currency slid nearly five percent on Tuesday.
The cabinet was also pondering a possible tax or a borrowing from the public -- steps which Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz wants to be voluntary.

His ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), the dominant coalition party, faces a challenge from an opposition alliance led by the Solidarity union in September 21 elections and handling of the crisis could have a bearing on the result.
The cabinet has already come under opposition fire.
The centrist Union for Freedom on Monday reproached it for failing to declare a state of emergency, which would have given it extra powers at a cost, by law, of delaying the polls.
A Solidarity chief, Maciej Jankowski, said last week: "The state has shown itself totally helpless and weak."
But Cimoszewicz said the worst, unexpectedly heavy rains were on Monday or Tuesday and by Thursday 20,000 state functionaries were involved in rescue efforts.
"I think any casual opinions about lack of action, lack of preparation...is not necessarily the truth," he told public radio on Tuesday. @
The premier said praise or blame should come later and now the main task was to clean-up and rebuild as much as possible in the next four or five months before winter.
Funds for this effort were already lined up and resources for longer-term work could be considered later.
He said it was hard to put a cash figure on the losses and provincial governors would report on material damage only.
"I am waiting for information about actual material losses, not money, because sums in billions of dollars will be flying in the air, and there is no real basis for this," he said.
